paper_title: A Broader Look into MLLM's Retrieval Heads

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Locating relevant evidence in long inputs is a core capability of Multimodal Large Language Models. Prior studies attribute this capability to retrieval heads, a sparse set of attention heads that transfer information from the context to the output. However, these analyses are confined to a limited set of modalities and the corresponding models. Moreover, how retrieval heads can be leveraged to enhance the model calls for further exploration. In this paper, we ask whether this mechanism expands together with the input modalities of the model. Taking audio-visual input as a newly added modality, we construct paired inputs in which the same answer is either spoken or shown on screen. With the evidence content fixed, retrieval heads remain sparse in the new modality and are shared to a large extent across modalities. Across 18 language, vision-language, and omni-modal checkpoints, omni-modal models largely preserve the retrieval heads of their backbones. Ablating these heads eliminates nearly all audio-visual retrieval. The heads shared across modalities make up fewer than 2\% of all heads, yet ablating them also degrades document understanding, spatial perception, and visual mathematics. Building on these findings, we turn retrieval heads into a target of optimization by training their attention with a ranking objective. This raises the page Recall@1 of Qwen3-VL-8B on MMDocIR by 6.03 points and improves document retrieval across three model families. Functional attention heads can thus serve both as a lens on multimodal models and as a target for improving them.

Functional attention heads can thus serve both as lens on multimodal models and as target for improving them. 1 1. Introduction Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) increasingly process long, information-rich inputs spanning growing range of modalities [17, 32]. Within these inputs, the evidence needed to answer question may occupy only small part of the context, surrounded by unrelated content. Locating this evidence is therefore central to multimodal understanding. As the range of supported modalities expands, understanding the mechanisms that enable this capability becomes increasingly important. Research on language models provides starting point: small set of attention heads, termed retrieval heads, transfers relevant information from the context to the output [25]. These heads occur across model families, and ablating them sharply reduces long-context retrieval accuracy. Subsequent work develops methods for analyzing retrieval heads [31] and extends this analysis to vision-language models, where visual retrieval similarly relies on sparse set of heads [13, 18]. These findings raise two questions. First, does the same retrieval mechanism extend to new modalities as models expand beyond text and images? This involves examining whether retrieval heads are shared across modalities and retained during adaptation. Beyond explaining model behavior, understanding this mechanism may also guide model improvement. Prior work has focused primarily on analysis, while how to translate these insights into stronger multimodal capabilities remains less explored. We therefore ask second question: can this mechanism serve as basis for improving multimodal models? To address these questions, we first study audio-visual input in omni-modal models. This setting allows the same information to be spoken or displayed, while related language and vision-language backbones allow comparisons across stages of modality adaptation. We construct paired inputs that place the same answer in long video as either speech or on-screen text, holding the background, question, and answer fixed (Figure 1a,b). Together with text and image-text retrieval tasks, this design supports unified question-toevidence analysis across 18 checkpoints. Targeted head ablations then test the functional role of the detected heads. We obtain four findings: Sparsity (Sec. 4.1). Retrieval scores concentrate in small set of heads for both spoken and displayed evidence. Cross-modal sharing (Sec. 4.2). Models largely reuse the same retrieval heads when the same information is presented in different modalities. Preservation (Sec. 4.3). Omni-modal models largely retain the retrieval heads of their language or vision-language backbones, and the retained heads remain necessary for retrieval. Causal role (Sec. 4.4). Ablating retrieval heads severely disrupts audio-visual retrieval. Ablating the subset shared across modalities, fewer than 2% of all heads, also substantially impairs performance on broader multimodal reasoning tasks. Together, these findings identify retrieval heads as compact, shared mechanism for evidence use, motivating direct optimization of their attention. We therefore turn to multimodal document retrieval (Sec. 5), where evidence localization provides natural ranking signal. We select retrieval heads on document-related tasks and use their question-topage attention to score candidate pages. ranking objective trains these scores to favor relevant pages over distractors. On MMDocIR [7], this improves Qwen3-VL-8Bs page Recall@1 by 6.03 points over the untrained scorer and also improves layout retrieval without layout supervision, with gains across three model families. Our contributions are threefold: paired analysis of retrieval heads across evidence modalities and related model checkpoints, characterizing their sparsity, cross-modal sharing, and preservation as input modalities expand. Causal evidence that retrieval heads support audio-visual retrieval and that small subset shared across modalities also supports broader multimodal reasoning. ranking method that directly optimizes retrieval-head attention and improves multimodal document retrieval across model families. 2. Related work Functional attention heads. Early studies identified retrieval heads as sparse, causally important component of evidence retrieval in long-context language models, using answer-copying behavior to characterize their function [25]. Query-focused scoring extends this analysis to attention between query and relevant context, allowing retrieval heads to be identified on realistic question-answering tasks [31]. Further analyses reveal the dynamic nature of retrieval heads in evidence retrieval [15]. In vision-language models, functional specialization has been observed in text recognition, spatial grounding, and visual evidence retrieval, with causal interventions linking selected heads to evidence localization and downstream reasoning [1, 10, 18, 21]. Functional head utilization. Despite growing mechanistic understanding, exploiting retrieval heads to improve model capabilities remains relatively underexplored. Existing efforts have focused largely on language models, ranging from attention-based retrieval and efficient inference to interventions that improve evidence use [12, 14, 16, 26, 31]. As mechanistic analysis extends to multimodal models, emerging applications suggest similar potential, but the broader use of these mechanisms to improve multimodal capabilities remains less explored [13, 19]. Building on this perspective, 2 we extend the analysis of retrieval mechanisms and explore their potential to improve multimodal evidence use. Table 1. Checkpoints used for mechanism analysis. Retrieval heads are sparse for audio evidence Finding 1. Omni-modal models locate spoken and displayed evidence with small set of retrieval heads. Figure 2a,b shows the score maps of two representative models under audio evidence. Most heads score near zero, and high scores concentrate at few coordinates in the middle and later-middle layers. Causal contribution of retrieval heads 5. Retrieval-head-guided document ranking Finding 4. Retrieval heads are necessary for audio-visual retrieval, and the heads shared by audio and visual evidence also contribute to broader multimodal tasks. Audio-visual retrieval. Following Sec. 3.3, we ablate the retrieval heads on held-out examples (Figure 5). Removing the top-5% heads eliminates audio retrieval in all four models and removes most visual retrieval at both background lengths. In Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, for example, audio exact match falls from 98.3% to 0, whereas matched random ablation leaves it at 96.9%. Robustness to the head set. The effect does not depend on the particular choice of the top-5% cutoff (Figure 6). The top-20 heads already remove most audio retrieval. The AV-shared heads, about dozen heads selected under both evidence modalities, also lower audio retrieval well beyond random ablation; in Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, they also lower visual retrieval, and their effect grows with context length. Transfer to downstream tasks. Ablating retrieval heads is known to impair downstream reasoning in vision-language models [13, 18]. We test whether the much smaller crossmodal subset carries this role, using eight benchmarks that span document question answering, visual perception, multidisciplinary reasoning, and visual mathematics (Tab. 2). An equally sized set of heads detected on natural-image retrieval serves as second control. Ablating the AV-shared heads lowers performance beyond random ablation on all tasks, most strongly on visual mathematics and spatial perception, and its effect exceeds that of the image-retrieval heads in 15 of 16 modeltask pairs. Cross-modal sharing thus singles out small set of heads that is central to evidence use well beyond the task on which it was detected. Section 4 shows that small set of heads carries questionto-evidence attention and that this attention is necessary for using evidence. We use Qwen3-VL-8B-Instruct [2] as the main model and repeat the experiments with Qwen2.5VL-7B-Instruct [3] and Gemma3-12B-it [8] to test whether the effect carries over to other model families. Training examples come from the MMDocIR training set, which provides page-level relevance labels but contains no layout-level data. The model therefore never sees layout supervision, and layout retrieval serves as test of whether page-level training transfers to finer granularity. Base and trained variants of each model share preprocessing and candidate windows, so their difference reflects training alone. Evaluation. Conclusion In this paper, we investigated two connected questions: whether evidence-localization mechanisms extend as input modalities expand, and whether understanding these mechanisms can guide model improvement. Using paired audiovisual inputs and unified analysis criterion across 18 checkpoints, we find that omni-modal models locate spoken and displayed evidence through sparse retrieval heads that are largely shared when evidence content is matched and retained from their backbones. These heads are necessary for audio-visual retrieval, and the small subset shared across modalities also contributes to broader multimodal tasks. This functional role motivates the design of treating retrieval-head attention as target for optimization. Training selected-head attention with ranking objective improves multimodal document retrieval across three model families, demonstrating how the mechanism identified through analysis can inform practical method. Together, these results connect the understanding of multimodal evidence use with its improvement in broader setting, positioning functional attention heads as both an interpretability lens and an optimization target.

We next apply the same training to the other two model families. The results in Tab. 4 show that it improves both granularities for all three models. Page gains are largest for the two Qwen models, and layout retrieval improves for all three. On four out-ofdomain benchmarks, scores change by less than one point, with small gains on some modeltask pairs (Figure 8), indicating the small effect of our training towards out-of-domain performance. Head-set size. Finally, we vary the number of selected heads and compare retrieval heads with equally many random heads (Figure 7). For every head-set size and recall cutoff, training improves the retrieval-head scorer; the largest gains appear in page R@1, where the base model has the most room for improvement. Random heads also benefit from training but remain far below retrieval heads, both before and after training. These results show that functional head selection remains important after ranking training.
